notes.2: This proved to be a straightforward question with many candidates ticking the correct boxes.
notes.3: Most candidates achieved some success with this question.
notes.5: Both parts of this question were challenging for candidates.
notes.6: Those candidates that produced good answers in this question wrote about ‘what if’ scenarios, and the impracticalities of building lots of different bridges rather than using models. Some answers included references to the fact that models were safer or cheaper but did not give sufficient detail in order to gain credit.
notes.8: This question was quite well answered by many candidates. The question is a ‘discussion’ question and therefore requires the candidates to give both advantages and disadvantages in detail. Many answers lacked the necessary level of detail. Many candidates were able to state that sensors could give a more accurate reading where humans could not. Many candidates related their answers to a loss of jobs, expensive to buy or maintain, and that sensors did not need a salary.
notes.10: This question was very challenging as many candidates misread the question and answered as though the internet banking was at home. In previous series this would have been the type of question we had asked. This question stated that the internet banking was within a physical bank and the advantages and disadvantages were to the bank and not the customer. Those candidates that realised this did well. The most common correct answer related to saving staff wages as fewer tellers were needed.
notes.12: This question was quite well answered, with many candidates giving the features. Some missed valid reasons for them. Some candidates did not understand the features of a GUI, namely Windows, Icons, Menus and Pointers. Some candidates gave benefits rather than features.
notes.13: Candidates often understood the question but sometimes did not give sufficient detail. Most of the candidates could identify either a work pattern or a health issue. Many of the candidates gave answers relating to loss of jobs, making work easier as computers do all the work, or having more leisure time. Very few gave answers relating to training, productivity, de-skilling etc. Some did, however, give valid reasons for the different work patterns and understood what they were.
notes.14: Overall candidates did well on this question.
notes.15: This question was quite well answered by candidates. They understood that proofreading checked for spelling errors, but did not always appreciate that visual verification needed the original source document to cross check against. Some candidates stated that visual verification checked that the data was correct when in fact it checks that the data has been copied correctly. INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGY
notes.key_messages: Candidates who performed well in this paper used specific and detailed language when replying to ‘describe’ and ‘discuss’ type questions. There has been an increase in the number of candidates using brand names to answer the questions. It is clearly stated on the front page of the examination paper ‘No marks will be awarded for using brand names of software packages or hardware systems. Occasionally, candidates may need to expand their answers onto other parts of the examination paper or onto extra sheets. It is important that the candidate clearly writes where the extra part is written and writes the question number on the extra work. Candidates should spend time reading a question thoroughly so that they are quite sure what is required in the answer.
notes.general_comments: This paper gave candidates the opportunity to give clear, concise answers. There was a good spread of marks for the paper. The paper covered a great deal of the syllabus. The paper gave all candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge and understanding of ICT using a wide variety of topics. The examination paper included a question on internet banking. In recent examinations we have set questions about using this at home; in this paper, the question related to using it in the bank, and this had an effect on the way candidates answered the question. It is very important that candidates read a question thoroughly before answering it. The vast majority of candidates were able to complete the paper in the allotted time, and most were able to make an attempt at all the questions. There has been some increase in the number of blank answers. When a question indicates a specific number of answers, candidates should only write one answer in each allocated space as only one is marked for each space. Candidates need to be specific in the answers they give, rather than using general statements such as ‘it is quicker’. Answers should be supported by a valid reason. All answers on the paper should relate back to the question being asked. As in previous series, there was confusion between a benefit and an advantage. A benefit does not make a comparison whereas an advantage does. For example, a benefit of a laser printer is that it gives a good-quality printout, whereas an advantage is that it gives a better-quality printout than a dot- matrix.
notes.1a: This part of the question was well answered with nearly all candidates getting it correct.
notes.1b: This part of the question was well answered with nearly all the candidates getting it correct.
notes.1c: This proved to be the most challenging part of the question, with few candidates giving the right answer of ‘hanging’.
notes.1d: This part was quite challenging for many candidates.
notes.3a: This proved quite a challenging part, where candidates were asked about the benefits of using a GUI. Some candidates wrote about the features of a GUI or gave answers that were not detailed enough.
notes.3b: This was less challenging than part (a) with many candidates providing good answers. Some candidates described a smartphone rather than giving characteristics. Some candidates did not read the question carefully and answered by comparing with tablets and laptops. Battery life and cost are not allowed as valid answers as they are too subjective.
notes.4a: Most candidates answered this question well by pointing out that the password was easy to guess or that it was too short. Quite a few candidates detailed that using this as a password would mean that Aaron’s account would be compromised by hackers rather than telling us why the password itself was not appropriate.
notes.4b: This was more challenging than part (a). It asked how passwords could be entered without using a keyboard. This required candidates to know how key-logging software operated. Key-logging software will still operate even if a touchscreen is used. The most common correct answer was the use of biometrics. Some candidates misread the question giving answers relating to firewalls, encryption or making weak passwords strong.
notes.5a: This part required candidates to describe how they would set up a new database and then how they would test it. In order to gain full credit candidates needed to describe both parts. Setting up a database was answered better than testing it. The question was misread by some candidates who explained the system life cycle.
notes.5b: In the use of parallel running, both systems are run together until the new one takes over. Some candidates produced vague answers that did not state the new system took over, by writing that a system took over. Some candidates were able to give good benefits and drawbacks, for example the old system was a backup and that the costs would rise due to two sets of staff. Candidates must give valid reasons for their answers.
notes.7a: Many of the answers lacked sufficient detail . There were many references to hacking without any explanation as to its relevance. Most answers that gained credit referred to the ease of searching for data or editing data. The drawbacks of using a database were less well addressed with many answers referring to hacking.
notes.7b: Some candidates gave examples of the fields in the database, which related to content rather than features, and some answers were vague. Some candidates misread the question and answered as though the form was online, giving answers like ‘help buttons’. Good answers included the need for adequate space for responses, instructions on how to complete the form and the use of tick boxes.
notes.9a: Most candidates were able to at least mention online data storage. Some candidates thought that the cloud was used primarily for back-up of their smartphone. Other candidates thought that the data was stored on the internet, which is too vague an answer as the internet is only infrastructure. This question produced many references to branded software and cloud systems, which cannot be credited. Answers relating to cost and limited storage were not allowed as these are too subjective.
notes.9b: Many candidates related this answer back to their own use of the cloud rather than the generic use of the cloud; as a result of this the answers were often vague and lacked detail. Many candidates were able to give good answers about the need for internet access and the monthly subscription charges. Some candidates mentioned the many copies being vulnerable to hacking and the difficulty in fully deleting all copies. Answers relating to hacking are correct, but more detail is needed as data is copied many times and stays on the cloud for long periods of time.
notes.9c: This was a ‘discussion’ question and candidates needed to give answers in sufficient detail. Most candidates were able to give good answers. Good answers included the fact that it is more difficult to forge biometric systems and that the owner had to be present to enter the biometric password. Candidates also knew that biometrics were unique to the person. One candidate gave a very good answer on the issues of reading the biometric using a scanner, this was not on the mark scheme but was awarded marks as a very good concise answer.
notes.11a: Email groups are quite a challenging topic for many candidates, possibly as they are not used that much. As with previous questions, it appeared that candidates understood the question but did not give answers in enough detail to gain the marks. Some candidates misread the question and answered as though it was about emails and not email groups.
notes.11b: This question was generally well answered. The question was related to analogue and digital data. Some candidates wrote that the microprocessor changed the analogue data to digital data.
notes.11c: Most candidates did well on this question. Some struggled with the flow of data within the control system thinking that the microprocessor lowered and raised the flood barrier rather than a motor or an actuator.
notes.14a: Many candidates were able to write down that rtf means rich text format but struggled with pdf. Often those candidates that wrote a description did not explain it in enough detail.
notes.14b: Candidates understood more what each of these formats were rather than their differences. Some candidates thought that pdfs could not be edited, probably as they had not experienced pdf writers only readers.
